_note: Stone tools: obsidian and flint are quarried, and a knapper strikes blades and tools from them (Complaint 618, part of 530). Figures are sourced to pages opened in the Complaint 650 passes; a derived figure shows its arithmetic.

obsidian_kg.basis: per tonne of raw obsidian nodules or flows broken free and carried clear of the outcrop
obsidian_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED. No obsidian-specific rate was found (searches on Sierra de las Navajas, Chivay and experimental obsidian quarrying returned no hours or kilograms per person). Taken by analogy with hand-mined flint, the nearest sourced figure: Grime's Graves, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grime%27s_Graves): "more than 2,000 tonnes of chalk had to be removed from the larger shafts, taking 20 men around five months, before stone of sufficient quality was reached"; "The medium-depth shafts yielded as much as 60 tons of flint nodules". DERIVATION: 20 men x 5 months x about 21 working days x 8 hours = 16,800 labour hours (the working calendar is the author's assumption) / 60 tonnes = about 280 hours a tonne of flint, counting the chalk dug through to reach the seam. A deep-shaft figure: flint from an outcrop or gravel costs less, so this is a ceiling. Where obsidian outcrops is a property of the map; no deposit is placed yet.

flint_kg.basis: per tonne of raw flint nodules dug from chalk or gravel and carried clear
flint_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED. Grime's Graves, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grime%27s_Graves): "more than 2,000 tonnes of chalk had to be removed from the larger shafts, taking 20 men around five months, before stone of sufficient quality was reached"; "The medium-depth shafts yielded as much as 60 tons of flint nodules". DERIVATION: 20 men x 5 months x about 21 working days x 8 hours = 16,800 labour hours (the working calendar is the author's assumption) / 60 tonnes = about 280 hours a tonne of flint, counting the chalk dug through to reach the seam. A deep-shaft figure: flint from an outcrop or gravel costs less, so this is a ceiling. Where flint lies is a property of the map; no deposit is placed yet.

obsidian_blade_kg.basis: per tonne of pressure-flaked prismatic obsidian blades, before use
obsidian_blade_kg.yield_basis: MASS: Sheets and Muto, 'Pressure Blades and Total Cutting Edge: An Experiment in Lithic Technology', Science 175 (1972), abstract read at https://vivo.colorado.edu/display/pubid_69138 : "Pressure techniques were used to remove 83 blades from a preformed obsidian core weighing 820 grams"; "The blades represented 91 percent of the original weight". So 1000 kg of blades needs 1000 / 0.91 = 1099 kg of preformed core, and a blade weighs about 0.91 * 820 / 83 = 9.0 g (about 110 blades a kilogram). The experiment starts from a preformed core, so the mass lost shaping a raw nodule into a core is added from Castaneda, 'A few good blades', Journal of Lithic Studies 3(2) (2016), PDF opened at https://journals.ed.ac.uk/lithicstudies/article/download/1435/2295/6648 : in the first reduction of a flint nodule "a 30% of the initial volume was discarded" (geodes and fissures). Flint is used as the analogue for obsidian, both being conchoidal glass-like stone; so a core is 70 percent of the nodule and 1000 kg of blades needs 1099 / 0.70 = 1570 kg of raw obsidian. LABOUR: John E. Clark, 'Prismatic Blademaking, Craftsmanship, and Production', Ancient Mesoamerica 8 (1997), abstract read at https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ancient-mesoamerica/article/prismatic-blademaking-craftsmanship-and-production/4DE4B3F54E0E94388CDDD6D11FD7AF52 : the Ojo de Agua workshop's "maximum level of output" was "26,000, or fewer, fine blades per year", "the equivalent of part-time work during a three-month period". DERIVATION: 26,000 blades / 110 blades a kilogram = 236 kg; three months full time (13 weeks x 40 hours = 520 hours) is an upper bound on hours since the work was part-time; 520 / 0.236 = about 2200 hours a tonne, core preparation included. Floor cross-check: Clark's 1979 draft (https://objects.lib.uidaho.edu/crabtree/CE_B3_F2-Item24.pdf) quotes Clavijero, "in one hour a craftsman removed more than a hundred", about 1100 hours a tonne for detaching alone. Gate: the tree node mat_obsidian_blade.

flint_tool_kg.basis: per tonne of knapped flint tools (hand axes, scrapers, flake knives, sickle flints)
flint_tool_kg.yield_basis: MASS: Finkel and Gopher, 'Size Matters', Lithic Technology 43(3) (2018), PDF opened at https://humanities.tau.ac.il/sites/humanities.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/all-units/%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA%20%D7%A1%D7%A4%D7%A8%20%D7%9C%D7%9E%D7%93%D7%A2%D7%99%20%D7%94%D7%99%D7%94%D7%93%D7%95%D7%AA/%D7%A2%D7%91%D7%95%D7%93%D7%95%D7%AA%20%D7%93%D7%95%D7%A7%D7%98%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%98/Finkel%20Meir/Finkel-%202018%20Size%20Matters.pdf : "a weight ratio of 1:4 between end product and knapping waste (or 80 per cent waste) is a reasonable expected measure of reduction efficiency" for Neolithic bifacials, so 1000 kg of roughouts takes 1000 / 0.2 = 5000 kg of flint. Wasteful end: Putt et al. 2014 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4938430, Table 5), cobbles of 7984 g reduced to cores of 364 g, 94.8 percent lost. LABOUR: Hand axe, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_axe): "An experienced flintknapper needs less than 15 minutes to produce a good quality hand axe"; a forum comment (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/bkjqfhKd8ZWHK9XqF/should-you-make-stone-tools/comment/TsYzcSL3oFfPtnqzJ) quotes David Miles, Tale of the Axe, at about 20 minutes. DERIVATION: 20 minutes = 0.33 hours for a finished core of 0.364 kg (Putt et al. Table 5) = 0.92 hours a kilogram, rounded to 900 hours a tonne; an experienced knapper's rate. Needs no technology: flaking flint is older than any node in the tree.
